fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The illness that came with a question attached", "body": "Dr. Moshe Daniel tells Chance Garton how myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition he was told could be fatal, twice brought him to his knees and twice handed him the belief he was living by. In 1996 a dialogue at the Option Institute, run by Barry Neil Kaufman and Samahria Kaufman, led him to the sentence because I need to be perfect. He says being asked what made him believe that was itself the cure. His breath opened, energy flooded his arms and shoulders, and he calls the healing spontaneous. The second bout, eight years back, exposed a karmic pattern about becoming a father."}, {"title": "From ninja books to naturopathic school", "body": "Asked for an elevator pitch, Moshe describes a childhood of rectangular white lights opening in front of his bed and the sensation of chi moving through his body as a teenager in the early eighties. With no framework for it, he read a book on ninjutsu and decided he must be a ninja. At fifteen he read Barbara Brennan's Hands of Light and wanted to be a healer with a foot in science, so he chose naturopathic medicine. He tells Chance the schools lost their way chasing credibility from the conventional model, leaving him hungry for what he calls the juicy marrow."}, {"title": "Beliefs get incepted, and the body obeys", "body": "Moshe's core argument is that the mind is the command center and the body simply enacts what it is told. He borrows the word incepted from the film Inception. He says he incepted himself with the thought that his life was over when fatherhood arrived, and that he sees the same kind of planted belief, such as you are nothing without money, play out in people in his practice. Chance adds parallels from his own biofield tuning sessions and asks whether ancestral patterns can make an illness hit harder."}, {"title": "Perfectionism, motherhood and the crying baby", "body": "Moshe separates healthy striving, the Japanese idea of shibumi, from perfectionism, which he calls compensation for not feeling good enough and a form of procrastination that even parks energy in the right ankle, the foot that would take the step. He and Chance then attack the collective beliefs nobody questions, the pressure on men to be providers, the refusal to honor a mother's work at home, and the advice to let infants cry it out so they can self soothe. He contrasts Finland, which supports a mother for four years, with two weeks in the United States."}, {"title": "Green allopathy and the case against diagnosis", "body": "Moshe teaches Holistic Counseling to practitioners and is opening the same material to everyone as Counsel Thyself, a weekend of dialogue technique built on never asking why. In his first book, The Revolution of Naturopathic Medicine, he argues diagnosis is a tool for allopathic treatment and does little for chronic illness, since a thousand migraines have a thousand causes. He deemphasizes nutrition and supplements, calls swapping herbs for pharmaceuticals green allopathy, and estimates seventy percent of graduates end up there. Chance counters that raising vitality makes the epiphany more likely, and Moshe grants the point."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dr. Moshe Daniel joins InnerVerse to teach us about Naturopathic Medicine! A true modern polymath, Moshe is versed in homeopathy, music, Hermeticism, and more. As an author and inventor, Dr. Daniel is thought leader in the world of mind-body medicine, and has written multiple books, including The Revolution of Naturopathic Medicine.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the 2nd hour, on InnerVerse Plus, we dive into the mystery of the Mem-Shin-Heh, aka Moses/Messiah/Moshe, we discuss astrotheology and the historicity of mythos, learn more about homeopathy and how animals, starlight, and planetary energy can infuse remedies, and how to use these subtle but powerful tools to willfully shift and expand our consciousness.
